opus-5.5.text:
So the core issue is that if you want to understand what a model is doing, the natural first thing you'd like to do is look at the neurons and say, "this one represents X, that one represents Y." And for the MLP layers in particular, that just doesn't work very well. The neurons are polysemantic. A single neuron will fire for, you know, academic citations and also Korean text and also some piece of HTML, and there's no clean story about what it's doing. The model is packing many more concepts into those layers than it has neurons, which is the superposition idea.

So the MLPs are where a lot of the computation happens, a big chunk of the parameters live there, and they're also the least legible part of the model. That made them the obvious bottleneck. If you can't read the MLPs, you can't really trace anything end to end.

What we did was train a replacement for them, what we call a transcoder, or in our case a cross-layer transcoder, which is trained to reproduce the MLP outputs but using sparse features that are much more interpretable. Instead of a neuron that means fifteen things, you get features that tend to mean one thing: "this is a rhyme we're planning," or "this is the capital of a state," that kind of thing. And because the replacement is trained to mimic the original MLPs' input-output behavior, you can swap it in and get a model that behaves mostly like the original, but where the intermediate steps are things you can actually look at.

The attention side, we kept largely as is for that work. Partly that's a scoping decision. Attention patterns are already somewhat more inspectable, you can see which tokens are attending to which, and replacing everything at once would have been a much harder problem. Starting with the MLPs gave us the biggest gain in readability for a tractable amount of effort, and it let us build these attribution graphs where you can follow how information flows from the input through features to the output.

It's not perfect. The replacement doesn't capture everything, there's an error term, and sometimes the interesting part of the computation is hiding in exactly what we fail to reconstruct. But as a starting point it got us from "we have no idea what's happening in there" to "we can actually trace a meaningful fraction of the mechanism for specific prompts," which felt like the right first step.

r001.rationale: The response says replacing MLPs provided the biggest gain in readability and enabled tracing a meaningful fraction of mechanisms for specific prompts.

r002.rationale: It notes that attention was left largely unchanged and was more inspectable, but does not identify attention as the next interpretability gap after MLP replacement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way to think about it is that if you look at a transformer, there are really two big pieces doing the work: there's attention, which moves information around between positions, and there are the MLPs, these big feed-forward layers, which is where a lot of the actual computation happens. And a lot of the parameters of the model live in the MLPs. So if you want to understand what the model is doing, the MLPs are a pretty natural place to start.

The problem is that MLPs are hard to read. You've got, say, thousands of neurons in a layer, and when you look at any individual neuron, it tends to be polysemantic. It fires on a bunch of unrelated things at once. So you can't just go neuron by neuron and say "this one is the Golden Gate Bridge neuron." The model is packing more concepts into the layer than it has neurons for, and it does that through superposition.

So our approach was basically: let's replace the MLP with something that does roughly the same computation but is built to be interpretable. That's where the transcoders and the cross-layer transcoders come in. You train a much wider, sparse layer that takes the same input as the MLP and tries to reproduce its output, but with the constraint that only a small number of features are active on any given token. And when you do that, the features you get tend to be monosemantic. Each one corresponds to something you can actually name.

And the reason that's the right starting point, rather than, say, attention, is that once you've got interpretable features in place of the MLP, you've got the nodes of a graph. You can trace how a feature in one layer causes features in later layers to activate, and eventually causes the output. That's what lets you build attribution graphs and actually follow the model's reasoning step by step. Attention is still there and still matters, but in that framework you can treat the attention patterns as fixed for a given prompt and focus on the flow of information through these features. So it gave us a tractable foothold on the whole circuit, which is really what we were after.

r001.rationale: The response says MLP replacement made interpretable features and attribution graphs possible, providing a tractable way to follow the model’s computation and reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says attention still matters and can be treated as fixed, but does not identify attention as the next interpretability gap after replacing MLPs.

astra-6.text:
The MLPs were a natural starting point because they do a lot of the model’s computation, but that computation is difficult to interpret directly. You can look at individual neurons, but a neuron doesn’t necessarily correspond to one clean concept. It can participate in several different things, and a concept can be spread across many neurons.

So the idea was to replace that computation with something that approximates the same behavior but is easier to inspect: a much larger set of features, only a small number of which are active on any given input. That gives us a better chance of understanding what each feature represents and tracing how those features influence the model’s answer. The important caveat is that it’s an approximation—we still have to check how faithfully it captures what the original model is doing.

r001.rationale: The response explains why MLPs were a useful target and how replacing them could aid understanding, but it does not say that this work offered substantial empirical insight.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify attention as the next interpretability gap.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to find a useful unit of analysis inside the model. Individual neurons are often hard to interpret because they respond to several unrelated things. Our hypothesis was that the model represents more features than it has neurons, so those features get mixed together—a phenomenon called superposition.

MLPs were a natural place to start because we could study their activations without having to explain the entire transformer at once. The idea was to use a sparse autoencoder to reconstruct those activations with a larger set of features, only a few of which are active on any given input. That gives you a chance to separate concepts that were mixed together in the original neurons.

And reconstruction gives you a concrete constraint: you’re not just finding patterns that look interesting; you’re trying to preserve the information the model actually uses. That made it a tractable starting point for getting interpretable features and then investigating their role in the model’s behavior.

r001.rationale: It says MLPs were a natural, tractable starting point for finding interpretable features, but does not say this choice offered substantial empirical insight.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify attention as the next interpretability gap.
